description: Cluster one (red-colored, right) clarifies mostly empirical but limitedly conceptual research of customer emotions, concentrating on negative emotions confronted with unfavorable service experiences (Tronvoll, 2011). In particular, recent research on negative emotions revealed anger as a predominant customer emotions in a response to service failure (e.g. Funches, 2011; Hsu et al., 2021; Kalamas et al., 2008; Smith, 2006). HarrisonWalker (2019) also found frustration as another predominant emotion confronted by customers following a service failure. The documents also identified recent moderating (i.e. technology anxiety, relational benefits, and gender) (e.g. Hsu et al., 2021; Kalamas et al., 2008) and mediating variables (i.e. perceived betrayal) (e.g. Lee et al., 2013) on the customers’ negative emotions. The mobile service industry and hospitality industry (i.e. restaurants and hotels) are the research contexts where a recent academic attempt has more focused on this cluster.

The second cluster (green-colored, center left) consists of journal articles associated with employee emotions. Scholars examined how customers’ emotional reactions (e.g. aggression) affect employee outcomes, such as satisfaction and turnover intention. Such emotions as job anxiety have also been considered boundary conditions in this relationship (e.g. Raza et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2020). Research also examined emotional mediation mechanisms (e.g. envy, anger, anxiety) in the relationships between employees and customers (e.g. Chan et al., 2019; Tan et al., 2020).

The third cluster (blue-colored, left) includes research documents focusing on ‘brand love’, customers’ emotional reactions to a brand. The vast majority of articles within the cluster synthesize antecedents (e.g. brand reputation, hedonism, perceived luxury value, brand trust, and satisfaction) and consequences of brand love (e.g. brand loyalty, advocacy, willingness to pay more, positive WOM) in the hospitality context (e.g. Drennan et al., 2015; Kang, 2018; Liu et al., 2018; Song et al., 2019).

The fourth cluster (yellow-colored, bottom) consists of empirical research that addresses the gratitude concept in the service encounter (e.g. Bock et al., 2016a) and attempts to discover the role of customer gratitude in building quality relationships (e.g. Jin et al., 2018). The concept of gratitude is considered as a favorable reciprocal behavior triggered by relational benefits, such as confidence, social, preferential, and Figure 3. Customer overall satisfaction, avoidance, positive WOM, and fairness are found as outcomes of gratitude in service contexts. The authors also examined gratitude as a mediation mechanism in customerservice provides interactions (e.g. Bock et al., 2016b; Fazal et al., 2017; Xia & KukarKinney, 2013)

The fifth cluster (violet, top) consists of empirical articles examining tourists’ emotional experiences in hedonic consumption contexts (destinations). Some documents focus on developing a destination emotion scale (e.g. Hosany et al., 2015; Hosany & Gilbert, 2010) and others examined primary customer emotions in tourist destinations, including fear and joy (e.g. Faullant et al., 2011), festival-specific discrete emotions (Lee, 2015), joy, love, and positive surprise (Hosany, 2012), and delight (Ma et al., 2013). The authors also examined the roles of those emotions in satisfaction formation (e.g. Akgün et al., 2017; Faullant et al., 2011; Hosany & Gilbert, 2010; Lee, 2015).

the sixth cluster (sky blue colored, center right) specifies empirical documents examining customer delight. Even though the last cluster’s articles were less in number, all articles associated with delightful experiences of customers and particularly clarify how relevant factors, such as surprise moderate the influence of extra value on customer delight (e.g. Ludwig et al., 2017). Authors have also revealed potential antecedents of customer delight, such as joy, gratitude, and surprise (e.g. Ball & Barnes, 2017; Barnes et al., 2016).
